title: Hope
hook: hope that is seen is not hope (Romans 8:24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, disasters: the tower in Siloam, mercies new every morning, and Nehemiah's let us rise up and build. Your line was rebuild.

These have been heavy days. Failure. Growing old. A child's death. How long, O Lord. War. Floods and earthquakes. One hard room after another. Now, at the end of it, one word Christians set against all of it. Not as a bandage. As a direction. Paul wrote about it to the Christians in Rome, and defined it in a way that sounds, at first, like a riddle: hope that is seen is not hope.
screen: `HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here is the riddle in full, in the King James words: "For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for? But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it." Nobody hopes for the sunrise once the sun is up. You only hope for what isn't here yet. So hope, in Paul's sense, isn't a mood that comes when things look good. It's what you hold when they don't. And look where Paul says this. A few lines earlier he describes the whole world in pain: "For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now." Travaileth: the old word for labor, for giving birth. Paul doesn't pretend the groaning isn't real. He hears it as labor pains, pain that is going somewhere. That's the shape of hope in this chapter. Not optimism, the guess that things will probably work out. In Paul's letter it's trust in a promise that God will finish what he started, and for Christians the resurrection of Jesus is the first sign of it. Paul's example is Abraham, who "against hope believed in hope." Against all the evidence, he kept hoping. And the letter to the Hebrews ties hope to faith: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." In Paul's letter, every one of those hard rooms has that unseen thing at the far end. Not a door anyone can see yet. A door Christians trust is there.
screen: `HOPE THAT IS SEEN IS NOT HOPE.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last few days, failure, age, grief, injustice, war, disaster, and choose the one that stayed with you most. Name one thing you hope for in it that you can't see yet, a healing, a reconciliation, a peace, and hold it like a seed in a closed hand, without arguing about how likely it is. If you pray, you can offer it to God in Paul's words, that we hope for that we see not.
Hope. In Paul's letter, the trust that holds on to what isn't seen yet, the way a woman in labor holds on to a child she hasn't met.
Your line: hope unseen. In Paul's letter, it's held hardest when things look finished. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians speak of hope in the resurrection at funerals, in the creeds and in prayers for the sick and the dying, and churches mark it each year at Easter and in the waiting season of Advent.
